chapter_theme: Natrinai 321 to 340: night meetings arranged by landmarks and dreaded for the tiger, bear and lightning on the hill path; velan rites mocked and mothers who begin to see; a wife's chest claimed as inheritance and a lover's hair weighed against wealth; the heron and the monkeys that keep their mates while men stay away; and Vaanan's Sirukudi made the measure of what an unfaithful husband has taken.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீள்வான் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: grassland, wild jasmine and kurundhu at evening, with a wife waiting at home

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the man, his task done, speaks to his charioteer (தேர்ப்பாகன்)

321.reading: His task done, the man tells his charioteer that at this evening, when the short-fleeced sheep of the red grassland turn home to the clear sweet sound of their bells, brahmin women wear the wide-mouthed wild jasmine at the edge of the slope and the sun's rays sink into the rock, his finely-jewelled wife may be grieving quietly as she looks at the dull empty house; so drive fast, for as the low kurundhu-flowered hillocks go by, the trees of the old noisy town come into view.
321.nuance: The flock going home with its bells is the evening's picture of return, and it makes the house he imagines, empty and dull, the sharper: he reads his own lateness in the scene before he names her grief, and the urging of the chariot follows from it.

colophon.thurai: தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது தலைமகள் பாங்கிக்கு உரைத்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: a hill cleft with a tiger, and the velan's rite for a girl's love-sickness

comparisons.tenor: the tangled thicket in the hill cleft

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem addresses the hearer as தோழி

322.reading: The speaker asks her friend, so the man nearby may hear, whether it is true that if the sickness were eased that way nothing anywhere would be crueller: for the grievous longing that paled the girl's fine brow, because she cannot rightly have the cool fragrant chest of the man of the land where a fierce sword-striped tiger crouches at the narrow track men use to ease the hunger of its flesh-eating mate in a thicket-choked cleft, the velan has declared to be a spirit's work, singing to sweet instruments and scattering many flowers as an offering of praise.
322.nuance: The friend's scorn falls on the velan's diagnosis: the cause is a man's chest, and a rite to a spirit cannot reach it. The tiger that waits at the men's track to feed its mate keeps the danger of the night path in view; read as the man who should provide for his mate it is a near miss for iraicchi, since the act carries no single sense the closing lines confirm. How lines 1 and 2 bear on the rest is not certain.

colophon.thurai: தோழி இரவுக்குறி நேர்ந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: palmyra, punnai and sand dune of a shore hamlet

comparisons.tenor: the wind-ripples on the sand dune

323.reading: Agreeing to a night meeting, the friend tells the man that the tall sweet-toddy palm stands in the very middle of the small shore hamlet of the father of the bangled girl who, unknown to her companions and to the friend, set aside their fine friendship and took kinship with him; there, where bees humming with honeybees over the heavy pollen the punnai sheds on the tiger-striped dune make sweet music, the bells of his strong chariot will hardly be heard: this is the way to come, and he must not forget it.
323.nuance: The friend gives a route by landmarks, and her real point is practical: the hum of the punnai grove will cover the chariot bells, so he can come unheard. Lines 3 to 5 (the companions and I not knowing, the friendship set aside) are hard to construe and the sense of புலி வரிபு is not certain.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொல்லியது இடைச் சுரத்துக் கண்டோர் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone with her lover through elephant forest and the speaker grieves for the mother left behind

comparisons.tenor: the sheen of the father's strong-shafted spear

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: onlookers on the wasteland road, speaking among themselves

324.reading: Alas, pitiable is the mother: crushed by grief, what will become of her who loved her gold-bodied daughter, now that this girl of lovely sparse locks, who in her rich father's wide house of oil-sheened strong spears ran about as if chasing a ball at play, walks on her soft cotton-like feet through a forest full of full-tusked elephants?
324.nuance: The pity goes not to the girl, who still runs as at play, but to the mother at home, so the elopement is weighed by what it costs the house left behind. The colophon's thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but nothing of the poem's situation belongs to the hill tryst.

colophon.thurai: தோழி செலவு அழுங்குவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the friend begs the man not to set out across the forked paths of the wasteland

ullurai.tenor: the man going after wealth and the fresh beauty his going will ruin

pairs.situation: he leaves driven by desire for gain

pairs.scene: நீடு செயல் சிதலைத் தோடு புனைந்து எடுத்த
pairs.situation: the slowly built mound is her fresh beauty, which his going will undo
the ruin is done at one stroke, as her tears spoil her eyes

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a bear met on the forked paths the man must cross, a thing of the poem's own road (porul 7.27)

325.reading: The friend asks the man whether it is fitting for him to cross the hard forked paths where a bent-headed thick-haired male bear, eager for food, goes out at night and with rough mouth and strong claws tears open the snake-haunted termite mound that long-working termites built up in layers, even after seeing tears swell from her flower-like kohl eyes and spoil their fresh beauty; lord, give up your going.
325.nuance: The bear wrecks in a moment what the termites built over a long time, which is what the friend says his going will do to the girl's new beauty; she never draws the match herself.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவுகடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: a jackfruit slope with monkeys, and the forest where the girl roams

comparisons.vehicle: நுண் கொடிப் பீரத்து ஊழ் உறு பூ
comparisons.tenor: the pallor spreading over the girl
her eyes, which the bees take for flowers

326.reading: Pressing the man to marry, the friend tells the lord of the land where, on the fruitful jackfruit slope, a fluff-headed female monkey sneezes, unable to bear the smell of the fish the heron flock bring onto the dark fruit-laden branch, that she is ashamed to say it even to him: for many days pallor has spread over the girl like the ripe flower of the fine-stemmed peerkku, alas, while even the bees, knowing no better, take her eyes for flowers and come to them when she enters their lovely forest.
326.nuance: The pallor and the eyes the bees mistake for flowers are set side by side: her beauty is fading and still draws the bees, so the time to marry her is now. The herons' fish smell on the jackfruit slope, which the monkey cannot bear, may suggest gossip reaching the hill, but no second correspondence is anchored in the poem, so it stays scene (a near miss for ullurai).

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்தொழுக ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் வன்புறை எதிர் அழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: punnai over the shore grove of the lord of the cool shore

327.reading: Answering her friend's reassurance, the girl says that if trusting the sought-after noble ones is a fault, then wasting away with eyes that weep without rest, and even dying, is sweet, dear friend; and if it is not so, since the noble never fall short of what they owe, it is right that the soft chest of the lord of the cool shore, where punnai with opening buds stands over the grove, should become her settled inheritance, which the world gathered together will acknowledge.
327.nuance: She puts it as all or nothing: either her trust was a fault and death is sweet, or he is truly one of the noble and his chest is her lawful portion. The word தாயம், inheritance, gives the marriage she wants the standing of a property claim acknowledged in public.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வரைவிடை ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளை வற்புறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarded from parrots on the great hill slope

328.reading: Comforting the girl in the wait before marriage, the friend says they have come to know that the lord of the great hill land, where tubers go down and honey hangs above and a little sown yields much as people drive parrots from the millet, is not of a birth apart from theirs; so may the clouds one day gather and rise to the right and pour great rain and flood; and now, in this town on the high sandal-covered slope among cross-lying ranges, the virali who receives ornaments dances, asking for no sesame oil or white cloth.
328.nuance: The hill where little sown yields much reads as a promise for the union, and the dancing virali points to the wedding festival the friend says is near; but the sense of பிறப்பு ஓரன்மை (line 4) and why she wishes for the flood are hard to fix.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகளைத் தோழி பருவம் காட்டி வற்புறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: a wasteland road watched by robbers

329.reading: The friend comforts the wasting wife: though he has crossed the wasteland where greedy men who care nothing for hell kill travellers and leave them, where an old spotted vulture, finding no room by the reeking corpses, flaps out the broken down of its wings, and hard-eyed men whose red arrows are fletched with it lie watching the track with their hearts set on plunder, he will not stay away forsaking her; look there, the dark clouds have drawn up the sea and flash, shaking the vast sky.
329.nuance: The friend sets the road's horrors and the season's sign side by side, so that the rain clouds, the time he named for his return, answer the fear the road raises.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகனை வாயில் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: buffalo, pond and marutham tree of a rich town

ullurai.tenor: the man, his other women and the household he disturbs

pairs.scene: நெடு நீர்த் தண் கயம் துடுமெனப் பாய்ந்து
pairs.situation: he plunges into the company of other women
the household is scattered by his doings

pairs.scene: இருள் புனை மருதின் இன் நிழல் வதியும்
pairs.situation: after his pleasure he would rest at ease in the wife's house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the buffalo of the marutham pond in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

330.reading: Refusing the man entry, the friend tells the lord of the rich town, where a wide-horned rough-necked dark male buffalo plunges with a splash into the deep cool pond, scattering the many flocks of soft-stepping herons, and rests from the day's labour in the sweet shade of the marutham tree whose far branches are clothed in darkness, that even if he brings his finely-jewelled women into their house and embraces them, truth in their mean hearts is rare, and rarer still that they should bear sons as the green-bangled wives do and stand on the household's side in good and grateful chastity.
330.nuance: The friend grants the worst, that he brings the other women home, and argues past it: what she denies them is the household's virtues, truth, children and karpu, so the refusal is a judgement on them more than a plea to him.

colophon.thurai: தோழி இரவுக்குறி நேர்ந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: salt pans, salt carters and fishing boats of the sea shore

331.reading: Agreeing to a night meeting, the friend tells the lord of the cool sea, where salt-makers who never plough keep guarded heaps of brine-grown salt in the grove for the coming of the salt carters, and girls scaring birds from the drying fish climb up with their soft-eyed companions and count the strong boats of the kinsmen gone fishing, 'that is my father's boat, that is yours', that their faultless good town is sweet: if he comes now there is no wrong in it, for how would anyone come to know, when the town has streets where kin do not know kin?
331.nuance: The girls naming each boat by its owner show a town where everyone is known by family; the friend's last line turns it round, saying the town is so crowded that kin do not know kin, so a night visitor will pass unknown.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகளைத் தோழி களவுக் காலத்து வற்புறுப்பதலைவி கூறியது வன்புறை எதிர்மறுத்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: a tiger in the hill cleft on the night path he takes

comparisons.tenor: her longing that grows though he embraces her daily

332.reading: To her friend, who keeps telling her in many ways that her bangles have slipped from their old place, the girl says to stop and asks what this can be called: like people who gather water-lilies and still thirst for water, her shoulders waste though he embraces her day after day; and how can her shining bangles stay tight when she sees him come through thick darkness night after night, no longer heeding as on the first day, by the small path at the mountain foot where a dark strong tiger that has sheltered its newly delivered mate in a rock cleft prowls for prey?
332.nuance: The wasting is not from his absence but from fear for him: she has him every day and still pines, because every meeting means the tiger's path at night. பேணலன் may mean that he no longer heeds the danger or that he cares for her less than on the first day; the reading takes the first.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிவின்கண் ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: a wasteland the rains have left, crossed for wealth

333.reading: The friend tells the grieving wife to let her sorrow go: her lover, who went far for rare wealth wanting the means to give, and who does not call hard the wasteland where, after the clouds have ended their work and the bamboo has lost its beauty along the stony path, a tiger fights the spot-browed elephant to drink at the little seep in a pebbled hollow, now seems, his resolve worn down and his heart full, ready to come back to her embrace and have her fine-jewelled bamboo shoulders; for the lizard of pleasing voice, clinging to the bright wall of their high famous house, chirps at deep midnight each time she thinks of him.
333.nuance: The comfort rests on a household omen, not on news: the lizard answering each of her thoughts is taken to show that the absent man is turning home. The motive the friend gives him is வண்மை, wealth sought so that he can give.

colophon.thurai: தோழி இரவுக்குறி முகம் புக்கது

thinai_evidence.note: monkeys, vengai and falls of the hill, and the night meeting

iraicchi.act: the troop of female monkeys bathes in the falls, swings on the bamboo and frolics together with their male by day
iraicchi.sense: the lovers of this hill should have their joy together openly, as the monkeys do, not by a lone night journey through rain and lightning

334.reading: The friend asks the girl what would become of their dear life if the lord of the hill land, where a big red-faced troop of black-fingered female monkeys bathe in the falls of the high range, swing on tall bamboo and frolic with their male while the fragrant vengai blossoms that adorn the hill drop into the rock pool, should come at midnight in the dense dark of lingering rain, bearing a single spear along the slope of falls by the light of the splitting lightning.
334.nuance: The colophon says the friend opens the matter of a night meeting; she does it by voicing her fear of it, so that the girl's consent and the man's danger are raised in one breath.

colophon.thurai: காமம் மிக்க கழிபடர்கிளவி மிதூர்ந்து தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: sea, thaazhai, palmyra and anril of the shore at night

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks to no one named, to the night itself

335.reading: Overcome by longing, the girl says the moon rises in the shining sky, the surging waves of the roaring sea never stop their sound, the tide comes loud and goes, the wind spreads the unending fragrance of the thorn-leaved thaazhai in the flowered grove as its closed bud opens like an umbrella spilling rice, the anril on the dark palm calls in distress so that it pierces to the bone, and besides, a good lute plucked by grasping fingers keeps on so that the night cannot be survived: love is great, and there is no one to clear it away.
335.nuance: Every sound and scent of the shore night presses on her at once, and she names no man: the poem is the night itself closing in, ending in the bare statement that love is great.

colophon.thurai: ஆறு பார்த்துற்றுச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: boar, millet, hunter and elephant of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the friend is assumed

336.reading: Fearing the path, the speaker tells the lord of the tall mountain, where a hunter lying in wait at the hard narrow stony pass brings down with his bow the white-tusked boar that raided the thick-stalked millet with its slack-teated sow, and his wife of dressed dark hair cuts it up and shares it among the households in turn: you do not fear the night when the fierce elephant watches for the tiger, but I do; do not come by the small path at the mountain foot where a pack of bears hunting food dig into the snake's wet-holed mound.
336.nuance: The opening is a raid ending in a fair share: the boar that took the millet is killed and divided by custom. A reader may see the secret lover and the town's sharing of talk in it, but the poem anchors no such match, so it is left as scene (a near miss for ullurai).

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிதலுற்றானது குறிப்பறிந்து விலக்கியது தோழி உலகியல் கூறிப் பிரிவு உணர்த்தியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the man means to leave for wealth in early summer

comparisons.tenor: the gathered fragrance of her hair
the dark colour of her plaited hair

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem's vocative தலைவ fits the first alternative better

337.reading: Seeing that the man means to leave for wealth, the friend asks whether the great ones forgot, when the world was made: those who have made wealth have the custom of living apart, not taking the rare great gift of gently burrowing into her long fragrant five-plaited hair, coloured like sapphire, where the scents of early-summer athiral, the soft-haired dark flowers of thick-based paathiri and fragrant morodam gather as from an opened casket.
337.nuance: The complaint aims past the man at the order of the world: she blames whoever fixed custom for a rule under which wealth is bought with the very pleasure it should serve.

colophon.thurai: ஒருவழித் தணந்த காலை ஆற்றாத தலைமகள் வன்புறை எதிர்மொழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: adumbu creeper, palmyra and heron of a fishing hamlet at sunset

iraicchi.act: having fed on the wide sea, the heron flies as if its life would leave it to reach its mate's nest on the palm frond, never ceasing to call its partner
iraicchi.sense: even the heron hurries home at nightfall to the mate it calls, while her man, gone only a short way, does not come

338.reading: Answering her friend, who says she must hold firm against the grief that torments her, the wife asks how she can, when the harsh-rayed sun has gone behind the hill, the sweet sound of his tall chariot whose wheel cuts the adumbu creepers is not heard even by night, and, as dusk blurs everything, the pitiable heron that rose to feed on the wide dark sea flies as if its life would leave it to reach its curved-beaked mate's nest on the frond of the swaying palm in the commons of the fish-smelling hamlet, never ceasing to call its partner.
338.nuance: The heron's homecoming is the reproach she cannot say outright: the bird keeps calling to its mate as it hurries back, and the chariot that should come at the same hour is silent.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைவன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: secret love near to exposure, with the mother's suspicion, and a hill spring

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the poem's 'we two' points to the friend

339.reading: So that the man standing by may hear, the friend tells the girl that their mother seems to know the flood of distress the two of them swim, saying strange things with unsettled hearts and fearing 'will this not turn to gossip?' now that the unfailing lover has left them and shows no grace: the mother came into the fine great house, embraced her and said, 'tomorrow, so that this lightning-haired, bright-browed young girl in her wet petalled garland may get back her good looks, let her bathe in the clear gem-water spring in the fragrant hedged place crowded with flowers; what is this way of girls?'
339.nuance: The mother's plan of a bath to restore the girl's looks shows she has seen the change; whether she suspects love or illness is left open, and the friend reports it within the man's hearing so he knows time is short. Who embraces whom in line 6, and the tone of the mother's last question, are not certain.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் மறுத்தந்த தலைமகனைத் தலைமகள் நொந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: irrigated fields, vaalai fish and ploughmen of the riverine town

340.reading: The wife tells the man, back from other women, that she will not embrace him nor even sulk: he loosened her bright well-fitting bangles, precious as Vaanan's Sirukudi, where, when Chezhiyan of the unschooled elephants and swift chariots lets out the sluice water of his great tank, the vaalai fish with arrow-like spines meets the inflow, runs into the mud fields and, bold, flips at the base of the ridges of the green-stalked fields, struck by the ploughmen's sticks on its spotted white back where the bullocks kicked up mud.
340.nuance: Refusing both embrace and sulking is the coldest answer akam allows, since sulking would still be a lovers' game. The whole fertile town is spent on the bangles he has loosened, so what he has taken from her is measured by a king's wealth.

links.note: Natrinai 327's girl stakes her life on the belief that the noble do not fail in what they owe; Kural 990 says that if the worthy declined in worth the earth could not bear its load.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the failure of the worthy a cosmic impossibility, while the Natrinai girl turns the same belief into a private wager on one man, so the pair shows what the maxim costs when a single life rests on someone being counted among the worthy.

links.note: Both have a woman awake at midnight with a love too great to get past: the Kural's flood with no shore and only herself awake, Natrinai 335's great love with no one to clear it while moon, surf, wind, anril and lute keep the night going.
links.teaches: The couplet's 'only I am here at midnight' is filled in by the older poem with a crowd of sounds and scents that will not stop, showing that the woman's solitude is not silence but a shore night that keeps working on her.

links.note: Vaanan's Sirukudi, its fields and groves, is the vehicle for the wife in both: her hair smells like its groves in Akananuru 204, her bangles are as precious as the town in Natrinai 340.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show one patron's fertile town used as the standard of a wife's worth from both sides of a marriage: the faithful husband hurries home to a beauty like Sirukudi, and the wronged wife names the same town to measure what her husband has taken.

links.note: In both a bear digs into a snake-haunted termite mound on the path: in 325 on the wasteland road the man would take for wealth, in 336 on the hill path he takes to the night meeting.
links.teaches: The same bear tearing open the snake's mound marks the danger of the road away from her and of the road to her, so in the anthology the friend's fear attaches to the man's going whichever way he goes.

links.note: Natrinai 52 has the man refuse the 'life of living apart' (பிரிந்து உறை வாழ்க்கை) for his wife's athiral-and-paathiri scented hair; Natrinai 337 has the friend say that wealth-makers by custom live apart (பிரிந்து உறை மரபின) and forgo that same scented hair.
links.teaches: The shared phrase and the same flowers show the choice put in fixed terms, and the pair tempers the friend's complaint: what she calls a custom set when the world was made, the man of Natrinai 52 does turn down, so it is a choice and not a law.

links.note: Natrinai 66 is the mother at home picturing her eloped daughter on the hot track; Natrinai 324 is the man or onlookers on the track picturing the mother at home.
links.teaches: Each poem imagines the other end of the elopement: the mother sees only her daughter's eyes red with suffering, while those beside the girl see her running as at play and give their pity to the mother, so each grief misjudges what the other side sees.

links.note: In Natrinai 34 the friend tells Murugan he knows the sickness is not his affliction; in Natrinai 322 she tells the girl, within the man's hearing, that the velan has called it a spirit's work.
links.teaches: Together the two show the friend undoing the velan's diagnosis before two different audiences, the god himself and the hidden lover, and only the second can end the rite, by marrying the girl.

source_issues: 332: the colophon thurai runs two words together (வற்புறுப்பதலைவி for வற்புறுப்பத் தலைவி); copied as printed.
324: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem is an elopement through elephant forest with pity for the mother left behind; inferred paalai.
